analysis.one_liner: Replaces asbestos lawsuits with a no-fault federal fund paid by asbestos companies and insurers, and bans asbestos products.
analysis.headline: Referred to five House committees and four subcommittees, the bill never received a committee vote before the 109th Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The FAIR Act would have shut down asbestos lawsuits in state and federal courts and replaced them with a national trust fund run by the Department of Labor, paid for by asbestos companies and their insurers. Sick workers would file no-fault claims and receive fixed payments based on how severe their disease is, with fast-track handling for terminal cases. The bill also capped lawyers' fees, banned the manufacture of asbestos-containing products, and ended the fund's obligations if the money ran short. Supporters said it would fix a court system clogged with hundreds of thousands of claims; critics said the medical criteria and fixed awards would pay many victims less than a jury would, and that the fund might not be big enough.
analysis.who_benefits: Workers and families harmed by asbestos — shipyard and insulation workers, factory hands, and people exposed secondhand at home — would get guaranteed no-fault compensation without having to prove any company was negligent, plus expedited payment for mesothelioma and other terminal cases, a claimant assistance program, and legal help. Companies facing asbestos lawsuits and their insurers would also gain: their liabilities would be converted into fixed fund contributions and future lawsuits would be barred.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Asbestos victims and companies facing lawsuits

how_it_helps.text: Sets up a no-fault federal compensation system where claimants need not show any company was at fault, only that they have an eligible asbestos disease and sufficient exposure.
Creates an expedited process for mesothelioma patients and people diagnosed as terminally ill with less than a year to live.
Provides a claimant assistance program with resource centers, help preparing claims, and a roster of pro bono attorneys.
Bans the manufacture, processing, and distribution of asbestos-containing products, and prohibits health insurers from discriminating against people in medical monitoring programs.

analysis.who_pays: Asbestos companies and insurers, who would be assessed for the fund; and claimants, who would give up jury trials and potentially larger verdicts in exchange for scheduled awards under strict medical criteria.
analysis.who_pays_short: Asbestos companies, insurers, and some claimants

drawbacks.text: The fund's awards would be the exclusive remedy for asbestos claims, meaning claimants give up their right to sue in court and face a jury.

Strict medical criteria and an exposure-weighting formula that counts each year of exposure after 1986 at one-tenth its value would leave many exposed workers ineligible, and legal claims not filed within four years would be extinguished.
Attorneys' fees would be capped at 2 percent of an initial claim award, which could reduce the availability of legal representation for sick workers.
The bill sunsets key provisions if the administrator determines the fund has insufficient resources, leaving claimants with weaker remedies if the money runs out.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill offered real gains: guaranteed no-fault payments for people whose diseases take decades to appear, fast payouts for the dying, and an end to a court system that consumed money on litigation rather than compensation. But the same design served the companies paying into it — fixed assessments in place of open-ended jury verdicts — and the tradeoff for victims was steep: strict medical criteria, a four-year filing deadline that would extinguish claims, capped lawyer fees, and a fund that could fall short with only a sunset clause as the fallback. Whether victims came out ahead depended on details — the adequacy of the award schedule and the fund's financing — that would only be proven in practice.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was sent to five House committees at introduction, then passed down to four subcommittees, and sat there without a hearing, markup, or floor vote until the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. Mark Kirk introduced the FAIR Act of 2005 in the House on March 17, 2005, with five original cosponsors.

It was referred to the Judiciary Committee and four other committees — Energy and Commerce, Ways and Means, Education and the Workforce, and Financial Services — a multi-committee referral that splits a bill's provisions among panels with separate agendas.

Between April and May 2005 it was referred to subcommittees on Health, Workforce Protections, and Capital Markets, Insurance and Government Sponsored Enterprises, and no committee or subcommittee ever acted on it.
No further action appears in the record before the 109th Congress ended on January 3, 2007, so the bill died without ever receiving a vote.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Asbestos claimants kept full access to the courts, including jury trials and unlimited verdicts. Asbestos companies and insurers avoided mandatory contributions to a national fund, but kept the litigation risk they had hoped to cap.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Claimants and defendants kept the status quo

for.name: Rep. Mark Steven Kirk
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill on March 17, 2005 and delivered introductory remarks.

for.name: 9 of 232 House Republicans
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill, including Reps. Bass, Platts, Shimkus, Kennedy of Minnesota, and Dent as original cosponsors.

for.name: Asbestos defendant companies and their insurers
for.role: Industry coalition seeking a national compensation fund
for.what_they_did: Publicly backed national asbestos trust fund legislation as the solution to the litigation crisis.

against.name: F. James Sensenbrenner
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled a markup or hearing; the bill's action history ends at subcommittee referrals.

against.name: Asbestos plaintiffs' trial lawyers
against.role: Attorneys representing asbestos claimants in court
against.what_they_did: Opposed the bill, which would end most private asbestos litigation and cap their fees at a small share of awards.

sides.party_line_note: The House sponsor and all nine cosponsors were Republicans, and no floor or committee vote was ever taken, so the partisan split on this chamber's version was never tested.

industries.industry: Companies facing asbestos lawsuits (manufacturers, shipbuilders, insulation and construction firms)
industries.note: The bill would have converted their open-ended court liabilities into fixed fund payments and made the fund the exclusive remedy, ending jury verdicts. Their gain — capped, predictable costs — came directly from limiting what sick workers could recover in court.
An Asbestos Insurers Commission would have set insurers' fund payment obligations up to a specified aggregate cap, replacing uncertain litigation payouts with a bounded commitment.
The bill ends most private asbestos litigation and caps attorney fees at 2 percent of an initial award and 10 percent on appeal, eliminating the contingency-fee economics of asbestos practice.
Title V prohibits the manufacture, processing, and distribution of asbestos-containing products subject to exemptions, ending a product line that exposes workers and the public.
